args.text:
KEY MESSAGE 2...Isolated shower possible Wednesday, but drier overall. Then it's dry again for Thursday, and a bit cool for this time of year.

A trailing cold front shifts across the region Wednesday, with surface high pressure building in from the west through the day. The model soundings have more mixing in the boundary layer, which backs drier weather and westerly winds gusting 20-30 mph (30-50 km/h). Put that westerly, downslope flow together with 925mb temperatures of +17- 18C and you get a warm autumn day, tops in the 70s (21-26°C) in a fair few spots. There's a hint of a stray shower or two as a weak wave comes through, but it won't cover much ground, and with the lower levels drier it'll be a light shower or a few spits at most.

As high pressure settles in further into Thursday, the airmass dries out even more. Thursday's meant to be dry, but cooler than Wednesday. A cooler airmass will have moved in by then too, with 925mb temperatures about 10C down on Wednesday. So temperatures a bit on the cool side for this time of year, mostly in the lower 60s (15-17°C).

KEY MESSAGE 3...Low pressure system expected to bring rain Friday into early Saturday. Gusty northwest winds and below normal temperatures.

Now, the deterministic and ensemble guidance both have a stronger/deeper northern stream shortwave trough pushing across the Great Lakes and the northeast Friday into Saturday. This system's got synoptic support too: an upper level jet sits near southern New England, giving large scale ascent and advecting a plume of above normal moisture north into the region. That sets things up for rain right across the board. There's heaps of moisture, mind, but instability looks limited, so the chance of heavy rain impacts isn't great. Ensemble guidance has amounts mostly between 0.25 and 0.60" (6-15 mm), with the ECMWF and Canadian leaning wetter than the GFS solutions. Going by those particular models, closer to an inch (25 mm) is possible. And those bigger totals aren't out of the question if we can tap into better forcing with the warm front. The finer details, like exactly when the rain rocks up and when it clears out, are still a bit up in the air, since the guidance doesn't agree yet. Best bet is the rain lobs in the Friday morning timeframe and keeps on overnight. Most guidance has this system fairly progressive, so it won't be hanging about all weekend. The bulk of it likely clears out early Saturday morning. On top of that, the initial southerly LLJ with this system nudges in Friday, and if it mixes down enough it'll bring breezy to gusty southerly winds (gusts 20-30 mph, 30-50 km/h).

Then a strong cold front pushes across the region by early Saturday morning, putting the northeast in a classic cold air advection pattern: gusty NW winds, cooler temperatures and isolated showers. A NW 40-50 kt LLJ sets up across the region Saturday. The tighter gradient, and CAA to help steepen lapse rates, will back deeper mixing and so gusty NW winds. How much mixing we get and how strong the LLJ is are still less certain this far out, but the ensembles show a signal for gusts 35-45 mph (55-70 km/h), maybe more across the coastal waters. 925mb temperatures range between - 2C to +2C Saturday, likely making it the coldest day of the season so far. Tops'll likely battle to get out of the 40s (4-9°C) across the interior, with low 50s (10-12°C) in the valleys and on the coastal plain. RH fields show leftover moisture in the cyclonic flow pattern, which may be enough for some isolated showers. Some of the higher spots across the Berkshires may only hit the 40 degree mark (4°C) on Saturday. Bit early to say the "S word" just yet (snow). But...if the timing lines up, a morning flurry or shower can't be ruled out in those higher spots out west. Saturday night'll be a cold one, with good odds of the interior getting down to freezing at least. The higher spots may drop into the upper 20s (-2 to -3°C).

warnings.why: said 3 times; vary it unless it is the text's own refrain

result.scope: Issues: flagged phrases, swearing over the cap, US spelling and US words. Warnings: the guide's style rules and swearing density; fidelity to the original (length, names, numbers). Not checked: invented slang.

declined.reason: Takes 'A cooler airmass' (comparative adjective, colder air) as the noun 'a cooler' (an insulated box).
'northern stream' is the jet stream branch, a meteorological term of art, not a watercourse.
'Highs will struggle to get out of the 40s' means the temperature barely rises, not going through hard times.
'RH fields' are relative-humidity data fields in the model output, not fenced fields.
